title: Five Analogies That Explain UX
intro: The fastest way to explain a UX concept is to borrow an everyday object, in Don Norman's tradition. Each one is instantly relatable — which is exactly why it persuades.

learn.title: Doors, ramps and spice racks
learn.text:
**Push-or-pull door** — affordance is what's possible; the signifier is the cue that tells you which.

**Curb ramp** — built for wheelchairs, used by everyone with a pram, a suitcase or a delivery trolley. Accessibility helps all.

**Unlabeled spice rack** — identical jars look tidy, but you have to remember which is which. Label your controls.

try.q: Which concept does the unlabeled spice rack explain?
try.explain: Identical jars look tidy and force you to remember — like icon-only controls.

learn.title: The missing screw and the express lane
learn.text:
**IKEA missing screw** — you discover it halfway through assembly. Information belongs at the moment of need, not in a manual up front.

That's the form telling you a field was required *after* you filled in fifteen of them.

**Express lane** — “10 items or fewer”, with nobody enforcing it. Rules need mechanisms. If a field is required, the system should require it.

try.q: A form reveals a required field only after submission fails. Which analogy fits?
try.explain: Just-in-time information: tell people before they need it, not after.

learn.title: Triangulation, in metaphors
learn.text:
His 2023 set for explaining why one data source isn't enough:

• A winemaker who samples only a few barrels → small samples
• Reading only the reviews you agree with → confirmation bias
• A picture with missing puzzle pieces → incomplete data

Combine qualitative, quantitative, evaluative and generative work so each covers the others' blind spots.

try.q: Which metaphor stands for confirmation bias?
options: Reading only the reviews you agree with
Sampling a few barrels of wine
A door with no handle on either side
try.explain: You see only the evidence that fits what you already think.

test.q: What does the curb-ramp analogy illustrate?
options: Regulation drives better outcomes than research
Physical design is easier than digital design
test.explain: Built for wheelchair users; used by anyone with wheels.

test.q: In the door analogy, what is the signifier?
options: The cue telling you to push or pull
The fact that the door can open
The sign giving the opening hours
test.explain: Affordance is what's possible; the signifier tells you how.

test.q: What does the express lane with no enforcement represent?
options: Rules without mechanisms to uphold them
A queue that is optimised for speed
Prioritising frequent users over new ones
A shortcut that only experts discover
test.explain: If a field is required, the system should require it.

test.q: Whose tradition is Calabro following with these analogies?
test.explain: The Design of Everyday Things made the everyday object a UX teaching tool.

test.q: Why do analogies persuade so well, according to the article?
options: They remove the need for research data
They sound more professional than jargon
They can be drawn quickly on a whiteboard
test.explain: Relatability is the mechanism — and the reason to choose them carefully.
